articleTitle: Application issues for PWM adjustable speed AC motor drives
abstract: The development of advanced power electronic switching devices has enabled high-frequency switching operation and has improved the performance of pulse-width modulated (PWM) inverters for driving induction motors. Switching frequencies of 2 to 20 kHz are common with insulated gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) technology for power levels over 200 kW.

articleTitle: A voltage sag study in an industry with adjustable speed drives
abstract: Three fundamental changes are commonly mentioned as having a significant impact on power quality problems [1]: 1. Microelectronics is responsible for a growing category of loads (residential, commercial, and industrial) that are sensitive to variations of the power supplied. Large scale integration (LSI) and very large scale integration (VLSI) of modern chips have resulted in faster, more complex components. An additional advantage is more memory per unit surface, with less requirement of voltage and power levels, thus reducing energy consumption and ventilation needs. Unfortunately, the lower voltage levels are easily disturbed [2].

articleTitle: Modeling of low inductive busbar connections
abstract: The high power levels required by many power electronic applications—as well as the very low switching times encountered in new semiconductor devices—have created a need for low wiring inductances. The busbar technology is an effective industrial way to reduce the interconnection inductance between (for instance) the feeding source and the converter. It consists in a stacking of several copper sheets, each separated from the other by dielectric. The connections between these sheets and the different devices are made with screws. An example of structure will be presented below.

articleTitle: An AC power supply with sliding-mode control
abstract: Electronic AC power supplies are classic products in power electronics. They include uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), test supplies, and conversion apparatus connecting DC power sources and DC storage systems to the utility grid or to AC loads. There is continuing pressure for increased performance in these supplies: tight voltage regulation, low harmonic content, a wide range of load variations, fast response, overload protection, and fast recovery from faults. In the case of power supplies for testing AC devices and systems, the requirements are even more stringent, and operation at variable voltage and frequency is needed too.

articleTitle: Investigations of voltage flicker in electric arc furnace power systems
abstract: The increased number of mini-mills producing steel has generated a renewed awareness of the impact of electric furnaces on the power system. The popularity of DC furnaces has also contributed to the evaluation of their effects on the power system compared to the traditional AC furnaces. Electric utilities are faced with the challenge of providing high-quality power to all customers as well as high short-circuit capabilities to minimize the effects of large arc furnace loads.

articleTitle: Compact wheel direct drive for EVs
abstract: The envisaged introduction of electrical vehicles (EVs) in the market will open a large application area for electrical motor drives, and such a prospect is drawing considerable attention and substantial international activity toward the development of electrical motor drives that allow an improvement in the performance of EVs. Among a number of drive arrangements under investigation for application in EVs, one advantageous solution consists in the use of a low-speed electrical motor coupled directly to the wheel axle to eliminate the mechanical power transmission system otherwise required. Advantages resulting from such a drive arrangement are a significant reduction of the vehicle weight and an improvement in the drive's overall efficiency. However, the wheel direct drive application requires the use of low-speed motors having a very high torque-to-weight ratio and efficiency to limit the ma ss stressing the wheel suspension and really gain the benefits envisaged in terms of drive efficiency.

articleTitle: Reactive power demand of transformers with DC bias
abstract: It has been observed that the presence of DC bias currents/ fluxes in power transformers generates harmonic currents and voltages with an associated increase in reactive power (kVAR) demand resulting in a voltage drop [1], Such DC biases can occur □ in transformers near high-voltage DC (HVDC) terminals [2] □ due to imperfect or half-controlled rectification resulting in DC, even and odd harmonics □ because of geomagnetically induced currents □ as a consequence of nuclear explosions [3] changing the Earth's magnetic field, and □ due to rectifiers working in a normal (e.g., half-wave) mode.

articleTitle: Inverter-driven synchronous motors for constant power
abstract: Inverter-driven synchronous motors (SMs) are widely used in high-performance variable-speed drive systems. The typical schematic of an SM drive system is shown in Fig. 1. The armature current vector of an SM is decided according to the command (torque or speed) and the current-regulated voltage- source pulse width modulated (PWM) inverter drive's SM so that the instantaneous armature currents follow their commanded values. The stator and winding of SMs are the same as a standard induction motor, but the rotor configuration is different depending on the type of machine. Therefore, SMs can be modeled by the same d-q reference frame circuit and generally analyzed, where the machine parameters in the d-q equivalent circuit depend on the rotor configuration.

articleTitle: An integrated on-line motor protection system
abstract: Motor protection equipment is typically aimed at protecting the motor insulation against overheating. Additional protection can be gained by applying expensive equipment based on sensing vibration and/or the current spectra of the motor to predict incipient failures. These systems, which have only recently been introduced, have limited application because of the cost and expertise required to operate them. This article proposes a single, low-cost, microprocessor-based unit to protect the motor against—or to alert the user to—the majority of motor failure modes. The proposed system includes thermal modeling for overload protection and variable ground fault protection. Mechanical failure prediction using current spectral analysis is also provided using a frequency selective expert system and a neural network to distinguish potential fault conditions from unknown on-line operating conditions.

articleTitle: History [origin of the inverter]
abstract: David Prince probably coined the term inverter. It is unlikely that any living person can now establish with certainty that Prince (or anyone else) was the originator of this commonly used engineering term. However, in 1925 Prince did publish an article in the GE Review titled “The Inverter” [1], His article contains nearly all important elements required by modern inverters and is the earliest such publication to use that term in the open literature.

articleTitle: Distribution reliability: what is it?
abstract: Distribution reliability is a topic that has received attention from many different people, including CEOs, public service commissions, engineers, customers, and others. This has happened because distribution reliability performance directly affects customers. In this age of fierce competition, everyone wants to have their company in the top quartile of utilities in terms of distribution reliability performance. The key to reaching the top quartile is understanding distribution reliability; answering the following questions will aid in that endeavor.

articleTitle: A single-pass design method for high-frequency inductors
abstract: As the operating frequency and the power rating of power electronic converters increase, the design of high-efficiency inductors and transformers becomes more difficult. Many design procedures described in the literature make use of numerous nomograms, and several iterations of the procedure are normally required. There is a general perception that the design of magnetic components is difficult, that it requires significant experience, and that it even has elements of “black magic.” It has been particularly difficult to teach magnetic component design to undergraduate students.

articleTitle: PM motors for direct driving optical telescope
abstract: This article details the task of developing the drive systems for VLT (Very Large Telescope) control. The project entails the realization and the coordinated operation of four 8m diameter optical telescopes in Chile for the period 1995-1998 (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Power system compatibility with industrial process equipment
abstract: Who has the responsibility of preventing power-quality-induced downtime for industrial process equipment? Some say the electric utility should provide power free from abnormal variations. Others have said that manufacturers must build equipment that can tolerate any electrical disturbance. Perhaps users should design or specify their industrial systems to be insensitive to power variation. This article presents an overview of a panel of representatives from each of these groups discussing the answer to this question.

articleTitle: Single-phase voltage regulators and three-phase systems
abstract: Voltage regulators are applied on distribution systems to control the voltage delivered to customers within acceptable industry standards. Concerns about the quality of electric power delivered to customers by utility companies have raised the level of awareness of high- and low-voltage conditions at customer facilities. Normally occurring voltage drops through lines and transformers vary with the load level on the system. Voltage regulators, when properly applied, can compensate for these voltage drops and keep customer voltage within proper limits. Single-phase voltage regulators can be applied on three-phase systems in a variety of ways, including grounded-wye, open-wye, closed-delta, and open-delta. The capabilities of the regulator systems are affected by the system design. In this article we will review the characteristics of the closed-delta and wye applications, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each application scheme. The impact of the regulator connection on the overcurrent protection scheme will also be reviewed.

articleTitle: The universal overcurrent relay
abstract: A comprehensive list of non-directional overcurrent relays would include thermal overload, inverse-time, definite time, and instantaneous relays. The list could be further classified by operating quantities including individual phase, residual, and negative-sequence current. Taken collectively and depending on the characteristic shape, pickup and time range, and dynamics, these relays span the applications for motor, feeder, and breaker failure protection.

articleTitle: Power system grounding. II. RCD and GFCI
abstract: “The principle[s] of the Residual Current Device (RCD), as applied in the USA by the Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) and Ground Fault Protection of equipment (GFP), and related electronic creatures, are revolutionizing electrical safety in buildings.” This statement by Earl Roberts in his new book [1] warrants careful attention. His book raises many questions, the answers to which may be unexpected. RCD, isn't this a new term? What is the principle of the RCD? Who needs to know about RCDs? GFCI, what is that? Is it true that “electronic creatures” are revolutionizing electrical safety in buildings? If so, is it also true of other places occupied by people? Are there considerations other than human safety? What is the role of grounding in GFCI? Is it possible to utilize GFCI without also intentionally grounding the circuit to be protected, and vice versa?

articleTitle: Control of PWM voltage inverters in the pulse dropping region
abstract: With pulse width modulated (PWM) inverter control of ac induction motors well established, attention now focuses on problems that until recently were either overlooked or deemed inconsequential. Following the groundbreaking work of Stemmier, others followed with improvements in the basic PWM strategy to increase fundamental output voltage or, in the case of Plunket, apply the basic principles to current-regulated PWM (CRPWM) inverters [1-3].

articleTitle: Worldwide reliability survey of high-voltage circuit breakers
abstract: CIGRE 13.06 Working Group has conducted two worldwide reliability surveys of the reliability of high-voltage circuit breakers 63 kV and above. The first enquiry included 78,000 breaker-years of "in-service data" from 102 companies in 22 countries during the years 1974 through 1977 and included all interrupting technologies. The second enquiry included 70,708 breaker-years from 132 companies in 22 countries for the years 1988 through 1991 and included only single-pressure SF6 breakers because this is what most companies are now buying. Thirty-one U.S. utilities and industrials submitted data. Results are reported in [1, 2].

articleTitle: Computerized DC (battery) load flow calculations
abstract: The key to properly sizing cables, overcurrent devices, and batteries is correctly calculating load current. The load current for constant-power devices increases as voltage decreases. The opposite is true for constant-resistive devices. If the effects of voltage are neglected, the designer can over-design circuits for constant-resistance loads and under-design circuits for constant-power loads.

articleTitle: Origins of the Servo-Motor [History]
abstract: The name “Le-Servomoteur" or slavemotor was used by Farcot in 1868 to describe hydraulic and steam engines for use in ship steering [1]. Actual origins of the term are lost in antiquity, but Otto Mayr cites a book published by the Farcot family that contains the first printed use of this term [2]. In 1896, H. Calendar in England developed the first electric servo-mechanism, which was a contactor-actuated “follow-up” device for use with strip chart recorders [3]. In 1898, Nikola Tesla experimented with “wireless control" of model ships on the Potomac River basin. He also used electric contactor “servo-motors” to steer model ships remotely. (Contactor servo is another name for time-optimal or “bangbang” servo.) In 1908, Elmer Sperry used electric contactor "servo-motors” for his gyroscopic compasses [4], In 1911, Henry Hobart defined servo-motor in his electrical engineering dictionary [5]. In 1916, Lawrence Sperry filed a U.S. patent application for an aerial torpedo in which a “servo-motor” moved the rudder to steer the course [4], By 1915, the term “servo-motor” was firmly entrenched within the language of America's community of electrical engineers, and perhaps elsewhere. The term is certainly of French origin rather than English.

articleTitle: Mechatronical considerations in modern motorcar generators
abstract: In recent years the demand for electrical power in modern motorcars has constantly been increasing due to climatization; heating of seats, windows, and mirrors; and the supply of electrical servomotors in place of hydraulic or pneumatic servos. Even when standing in a traffic jam the power supply should be guaranteed; thus generators with higher output power are needed. This higher output power should be achieved without increasing the volume of the generator because the available space beside the combustion engine is limited. The usual way to meet these requirements is to increase the maximum speed of the generator.

articleTitle: Toward 99% efficiency for transistor inverters
abstract: With the advent of power semiconductor switching devices, static power converters have been finding increasingly wide applications in fields such as motor drives and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). In particular, inverters may play an important role in motor drive systems for electric vehicles (EV) due to the concerns about clean air in crowded cities. In applications such as EV, miniaturization of the inverter is desired from the viewpoint of minimizing the package size. One of the most effective ways of making the inverter smaller is to increase the inverter efficiency, hence reducing the volume of the required cooling fins. High efficiency is also required for making best use of the batteries powering the EV.

articleTitle: Protective relaying an medium- and high-voltage system
abstract: The on-line performance of petroleum industry operations, such as production and refining facilities, is directly affected by the medium and high voltage protective relay devices used and their settings. For this article we reviewed unusual outages, such as non-selective device operations during a fault, at different petroleum industry facilities. As detailed below, we found that changing some types of protective devices and modifying device settings improved both reliability and online performance.

articleTitle: Electric heat tracing design for impedance and skin effect systems
abstract: When a material is transported by pipeline at a temperature above its surroundings, it will lose heat. Insulation will slow the heat loss, but will not prevent it. Temperature can be maintained by adding heat to make up the loss. This can be accomplished in many different ways. Heating stations can be located along the pipeline to make up the loss at discrete points. The problem with this technique is that the product does not stay at a uniform temperature, and if flow stops the product could lose so much heat that it becomes unpumpable.

articleTitle: Power System Grounding Part IV: High-Resistance Grounding
abstract: There are several methods available to ground the neutrals of power systems. High-resistance (Hi-R) grounding was first applied in 1936 to solve a safety problem associated with operating large portable equipment used in open-pit mines [1]. Experience with Hi-R grounding immediately showed unforeseen benefits, including reduced damage at the location of the fault when one occurred. In due course, this observation came to intrigue power system engineers. Still, the concept of using Hi-R grounding for purposes other than safety emerged slowly.

articleTitle: Power system grounding. Ill. Large portable machines
abstract: There are several methods available to ground the neutrals of power systems. One of these methods, high-resistance grounding, was first applied in 1936 to solve a safety problem associated with operating large portable equipments used in open-pit mines. The problem encountered was to avoid exposing mine personnel to dangerous stray electric potentials. It was brought sharply into focus in 1935 when an operator was electrocuted as he tried to board an electric shovel. L.M. Frazee, an electrical engineer at Oliver Iron Mining Company, recounted the circumstances surrounding the tragedy and resolution of the technical issues confronted [1].

articleTitle: Safety practices in electrolytic cell line working zones: 1994 changes
abstract: In 1974 the Electrical Cell Line Working Group of the Chemical Industry Committee prepared a trial-use standard for Electrical Safety Practices in Electrolytic Cell Line Working Zones. Comments on the trial-use standard were incorporated into a full-status standard and published as IEEE Std 463-1977, IEEE Standard for Electrical Safety Practices in Electrolytic Cell Line Working Zones. IEEE Std 463-1977 was reaffirmed in 1987. IEEE Std 463 was used as a source document for Article 668, Electrolytic Cells, of the National Electrical Code (ANSI/NFPA 70); Part 1, Chapter 4H, Specific Purpose Equipment and Installations-Electrolytic Cells of the Standard for Electrical Safety Requirements for Employee Work Places (NFPA 70E-1988); and OSHA 1910.306(h), Electrolytic Cells. In 1991 a working group was formed to review and update IEEE Std 463.

articleTitle: Electrical hot working safety program
abstract: An internal review of the safety practices for a large Canadian chemical plant indicated that the established procedures for electrical hot work needed to be expanded and formalized. The practices were expanded into a comprehensive electrical hot work program that included a philosophy, controls, qualifications, and safe work methods. The program resulted in changes that improved on an adequate chemicals and plastics safety standard and a facility safety standard. Detailed definitions were added to the chemicals and plastics safety standard, and a mandate for an electrical hot work procedure for all electrical hot work activity was added to the facility safety standard.

articleTitle: Large induction motor anti-friction bearing selection
abstract: The majority of motor specifications utilize L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> life as the sole selection criterion for anti-friction bearings. At times, L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> lives in excess of 100,000 hours are specified in an attempt to prevent recurring field problems when the failures are originating from non-L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> mechanisms. In some cases these failures occur indirectly from over-specifying L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> life. Some general examples of this are as follows: □ An oversized bearing is utilized to obtain a very high L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> life, minimum load is not maintained, and the bearing fails rapidly from rolling element tracking problems. □ The bearing selection necessary to meet the L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> criteria is closer to its speed limit, demand on lubrication increases, and marginal lubrication, possibly due to poor grease selection or lack of relubrication, results in net loss of service life. □ A spherical roller bearing is utilized to improve L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> life, small design thrust load is actually much greater due to a combination of axial magnetic force, coupling thrusts, and misalignment, the axial to radial load ratio requirements are not met, and bearing lives achieved are relatively short. □ The bearing type is changed from ball to roller to increase the L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf> life. As a result, the relubrication interval drops, this increased maintenance requirement is neglected, and no life improvements are obtained. A successful bearing design requires the consideration of many equally important factors. These are discussed in the following text.

articleTitle: Modernizing a forty-year-old production plant
abstract: The electrical generation, distribution, and utilization system that evolved from supplying a 10 MW load in 1954 to a 130 MW load today has undergone significant changes. The original two 69 kV-13.8 kV, 10 MVA power transformers still exist but have been supplemented by two 20 MVA and two 15 MVA units. The original 3750 kVA and 7500 kV A steam turbine generators have been replaced by a 17.647 MW steam turbine generator plus a 115 MW combined cycle co-generation unit. Many large (greater than 10,000 hp) synchronous motors now operate where 500 hp induction motors were the largest motors in the original plant. Two 138 kV-69 kV 75/140 MVA autotransformers have been superimposed on the incoming power sources. A 69 kV bare ring bus now encircles the expanded plant and supplies electric power via several 13.8 kV substation buses and captive motor transformers where once only a double-ended 13-8 kV bus substation existed. New features to enhance safety, reliability, operability, and maintenance have been incorporated in the changes.

articleTitle: A case study of main service short time demand intervals
abstract: Prior to the introduction of the 1990 National Electrical Code (NEC) [1], restaurant service entrances and main distribution panels were sized by designers using Articles 220, 230, and 240 of the NEC, as are most buildings. Specifically, designers also used Section 220-20 of the code, which enabled them to apply demand factors to “kitchen equipment” loads to size service entrances, main panels, and feeders.

articleTitle: Standards: SPA System Exemplifies Future of IEEE Standards
abstract: On Oct. 26, 1995, at the Chemical Manufacturers Association Internationalization Conference sponsored by the Electrical Codes and Standards Task Group, Ben Johnson, speaking on behalf of the IEEE Standards Department, explained, “The Standards Process Automation System developed to support IEEE Standards activity will provide the most feasible entree for IEEE into regional and international standards developing organizations.”

articleTitle: Industry News: Pennsylvania Electrolech Center Advises Local Industry
abstract: A fledgling partnership between a Pennsylvania utility and a local community college is helping electric utilities give their industrial customers local access to advanced industrial expertise and technology.

articleTitle: Practical considerations of area classification: how for to classify
abstract: Defining the classification of a location or facility (Class, Group, and Division), while often a difficult and time-consuming task, is only the first of three separate and distinct tasks that must be performed by those who provide Electrical Area Classification. This first task defines the kinds of materials that are present in the location using the terms Class, Group, and Division. Both Article 500 of the National Electrical Code (NEC) and The American Petroleum Institute's “Recommended Practice for Classification of Locations for Electrical Installations at Petroleum Facilities” (ANSI/API RP 500, or “RP 500”) are used in this task. The second task is to choose electrical equipment and installation techniques appropriate to the Class, Group, and Division decisions assigned to the location in the first task; the NEC is principally used in this task. The third and final task in Electrical Area Classification is to determine the physical boundaries or extent of the areas that are influenced by the Class, Group, and Division decisions reached in the first task. The NEC and RP 500 are both used in this final task of Electrical Area Classification. This article concentrates on the methods used in the third task to determine the physical boundaries or extent of Classified Areas.

articleTitle: Selecting fuses for power semiconductor devices
abstract: Considerable documentation is available from fuse manufacturers [1-4] on current-limiting fuses as applied to the isolation and protection of power semiconductor components, but there may be misunderstandings when interpreting corresponding withstand data from the manufacturers of power semiconductors. Although the Joint Electronic Device Engineering Council (JEDEC) [5] has published methods for verifying non-repetitive surge ratings for thyristors and diodes, some updating is needed in order to take into consideration the substantial increase in power ratings that have become available since that time.

articleTitle: Electric railway traction in Europe
abstract: The European railway scene has undergone major changes in the lase five years. The scare-owned railway service traditional in Europe is increasingly going to be reorganized into a production sector responsible for train operation managed industrially- and, further on, into as care-governed sector providing the right of way and fixed facilities to give railway transport a fair chance co compete economically with individual road transport.

articleTitle: Report on enclosure internal arcing tests
abstract: The improvement of electrical equipment is an ongoing process including investigative research. This is a report on research work concerning factors regarding high-energy arcing faults, the tests conducted on containment of these faults, and standards addressing arcing fault test requirements. This report is focused on low-voltage, 600 V class Motor Control Centers (MCCs), but the issues presented should not be limited to only this type of electrical equipment. Also, the scope of this work is restricted to a high-energy arcing fault occurring in a latched or closed compartment during “normal” operating conditions and does not include arcing faults occurring in compartments when the compartment door is open.

articleTitle: High-speed, variable-speed drive system in megawatt power range
abstract: In this article we present an industrial application of a high-speed, high-power, variable-speed drive system with a rated power of 2300 kW at 15,600 rpm. The drive is based upon economical and reliable components such as thyristor-controlled current source inverters and the rugged and maintenance-free squirrel cage induction machine. We could take advantage of many synergies with the standard load commutated drive technique with synchronous machines. The installation of a capacitive filter in parallel with the induction machine enables load commutation of the machine side converter and in addition yields sinusoidal machine voltages and currents in a limited upper speed range. Thus optimal overall efficiency of converter and induction machine is obtained.

articleTitle: Power disturbance and quality: light flicker voltage requirements
abstract: Current emphasis on power quality has brought renewed attention to the old subject of light flicker. There is a need to review the technical basis for flicker tolerance curves used as guides to satisfactory installations.

articleTitle: Fast tripping of utility breakers and industrial load interruptions
abstract: Some industries are very sensitive to electric power interruptions and voltage sags, which are a normal consequence of the utility fault-clearing process. Typically, U.S. utilities will try once or twice to clear faults without blowing any tap fuses, which would require dispatching a trouble crew to replace. To reduce complaints and to improve power quality for critical customers with high economic impact of interruptions, some utilities have been eliminating fuse-saving practices on feeder breakers and reclosers. The impact on overall reliability and the number of interruptions is evaluated based on recent distribution feeder power quality data. Some degradation in overall reliability can be expected, but this can be minimized with judicious placement of line reclosers. Critical customers can expect a significant reduction in the number of interruptions. A value-based economic analysis, including both utility and customer costs, shows that the practice has a high overall benefit-to-cost ratio. The utility experiences increased costs, but these are frequently overshadowed by the potential customer savings. However, removing fast tripping may correct for only a small portion of the utility-related events that might disrupt sensitive industrial processes.

articleTitle: Suggested practices for reducing animal-caused outages
abstract: Power quality is a major issue for electric utilities today. Sensitive electronic equipment and computers are a part of daily life, and consumers are increasingly critical of service interruptions. In many cases, outages and nuisance recloser operations are the result of animal contacts somewhere on the system. Although animal-caused outages have been a fact of life for electric utilities since the first line was constructed, there is very little general information available on what methods and products can effectively reduce such outages. In an effort to provide electric utilities with a source of practical information, the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) and Southern Engineering have prepared a field manual on suggested practices and polices that can be used to reduce animal-caused outages on transmission lines, in substations, on overhead distribution lines, and in underground distribution systems. This article contains a summary of selected topics as they appear in the manual for the animals responsible for the majority of outages Some utilities evaluate their animal-caused outages as a percent of their total system outages from all causes. This method, however, will often understate the seriousness of the problem since animal contacts tend to occur at specific locations. Many utilities reported areas on their system where 80-90% of all outages were caused by animals.

articleTitle: Safety considerations for electrical heat tracing
abstract: Since the advent of electrical heat tracing over 50 years ago, many challenges have confronted industry to ensure safe and reliable heat tracing operation. Reliability of heat tracing systems can directly affect safety-related operations, such as fire protection and emergency eyewash and safety showers. As a good practice, the safety of process systems should not be dependent on the performance of a single component of the heat tracing system.

articleTitle: Regulatory impact on the application of AC induction motors
abstract: This article will identify the impact of current and future laws, regulations, codes, standards, and recommended practices affecting the specification, design, operation, and maintenance of electric motors. The intent is to provide the engineer with a user's guide to assure compliance. However, space will not allow for the itemization of details pertaining to these factors. In the future, engineers will need to keep current libraries of these materials and be aware of pending or proposed changes.

articleTitle: Capacitor overcurrent protection for industrial distribution systems
abstract: Many industrial facilities apply power factor correction capacitors to enhance their electrical system efficiency. Power factor improvement, power loss reduction, release of system capacity, and voltage improvement can all be achieved by applying capacitors in industrial plants. Protection of these capacitor banks against excessive overcurrents is a critical part of the safe and reliable operation of the bank.

articleTitle: Switch off your office equipment and save money
abstract: Although technological innovation will improve the efficiency of electronic data processing (EDP) equipment, energy will be wasted if EDP equipment is left running when it is not being used. Office EDP equipment is the fastest growing end-user of electricity, now consuming anywhere between 25 and 65 TWh per year in the U.S., and responsible for between 5% and 20% of electrical loads in office buildings (Piette et ah, 1991; Patel et ah, 1993; Lovins & Heede, 1990). Newsham and Tiller (1992) presented data that established that there are long periods during both night and day when desktop computers are switched on but not used, and that significant energy consumption and electrical demand savings could be achieved if the time when computers were turned on could be more closely tailored to actual use. These data helped establish the technical foundations for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's “Energy Star” office equipment energy efficiency labeling program. Further, our data showed that a public information campaign using reminder stickers produced only modest reductions in computer on-time, and that these modest reductions were not maintained over an eight-week period. We predicted greater and more durable savings from automatic power management, which we were still in the process of evaluating with field trials at that time. In this article we describe the results of field trials of an automatic power management device for desktop personal computers, and outline the cost savings that might be achieved if automatic power management were applied to office EDP equipment. We also comment on the future prospects and challenges facing the Energy Star program.

articleTitle: Selecting overcurrent protection for three-phase transformers
abstract: Transformers provide the electrical power that drives most industrial processes. Even though continuous service is important, situations may occur that require the unit to be removed from service to prevent damage to the transformer or connected equipment. Proper overcurrent protective devices are essential for the reliable operation of the plant. In this article, we will discuss protective system philosophies and illustrate the selection alternatives through examples. Transformer inrush currents, overload capability, the protective device performance for different fault types, winding connections, and the impact on operating concerns will be discussed. Our emphasis will be on transformers applied within an industrial facility that are rated 2500 kVA and below, where the overcurrent device is normally a fuse.

articleTitle: Refinery-utility collaboration to increase value
abstract: Severe pressures to reduce costs, improve reliability, and generate higher shareholder value have helped to promote a successful change in the relationship between a major Canadian petroleum refinery and a large electrical utility. The relationship has evolved from a traditional customer/supplier relationship to a new business approach based on collaboration.

articleTitle: Hibernia: the next generation of offshore platform control systems
abstract: CIE-computer-integrated enterprise-technically best describes the Hibernia's new Grand Banks, Newfoundland, offshore drilling and production platform. Designed and constructed in an era of oil company belt-tightening, Hibernia takes advantage of modern technology co achieve the goal of a safe, cost-effective control system design.

articleTitle: Commentary
abstract: The 1995 conference of the Petroleum and Chemical Industry Committee (PCIC) was a great success. I've been attending this conference since 1989, and each year it has been bigger and more rewarding. The technical program is excellent… papers are informative to the engineer in industry, even if not working in the petroleum and chemical industries.

articleTitle: From the Editor's Desk: A Time for Reflection
abstract: Since this magazine has been in publication for one year, this seems like an appropriate time to reflect on the first six issues and to look to the future.

articleTitle: Society News
abstract: Meet the newly elected officers of the Industry Applications Society for 1995. Help us support them as they lead our Society into the new year.—Ed.

articleTitle: Chapter News
abstract: Happy New Year! I am happy to report to you a number of successful activities: committee chairs nominations, Chapters Awards, Distinguished Lecturers elections, department annual workshop, and department organization changes. But first, on behalf of the IAS Executive Board, I want to welcome our newest chapter, the joint PE/IAS Uttar Pradesh Chapter, formed on Aug. 23, 1995. This brings the number of IAS Chapters to a total of about 82 worldwide.

articleTitle: Conference News
abstract: Nine hundred IAS members converged on the Hilton Walt Disney World Hotel in Orlando, Fla., for our 30th Annual Meeting, held Oct. 8–12, 1995. If you didn't attend this year's conference, you missed out on five days of tutorials, technical sessions, paper presentations, and a fascinating exhibit hall. Here's a taste of what you missed. In the meantime, plan early to attend this year's meeting in San Diego!

articleTitle: President's Message: IAS Annual Meeting
abstract: Although it will be old news by the time this actually appears in print, the major item on my mind today is the 30th IEEE Industry Applications Society Annual Meeting, which was held at the Hilton Walt Disney World Hotel in Orlando, Fla., Oct. 8–12, 1995. Having just returned from this meeting, I continue to be amazed at the amount of paper that can accumulate on my desk in just five days.

articleTitle: Awards
abstract: At a June 22 ceremony at the Westin Mont-Royal Hotel in Montreal, two IAS Members received major IEEE awards. John R. Dunki-Jacobs (PCIC & ICPS), president of Industrial Power Systems Inc., Lyndon, Wash., received the Medal for Engineering Excellence “for a career devoted to the development of and contributions to the engineering and implementation of industrial power systems,” and Bimal K. Bose (IPCS), holder of the Condra chair of excellence in power electronics in the department of electrical engineering at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, accepted the Lamme Medal “for contributions to the advancement of power electronics and electrical machine drives.”

articleTitle: Awards
abstract: The IAS Fellow Committee recognized 13 Society members as IAS Fellows in 1995. We commend these members, and encourage all IAS members to support the program. Here's more information on how the Fellow evaluation system works, both within IAS and in the Institute. — Ed.

abstract: Hand-book n. Abbr. hdbk. 1. A concise manual or reference book providing specific information or instruction about a subject or place.

articleTitle: Power Electronics, Book Review
abstract: Power electronics technology has grown vigorously as a major discipline in electrical engineering in recent years. As the cost of power electronics apparatus decreases and its performance improves, it is gradually finding widespread applications in industrial, commercial, residential, aerospace, military, and utility sectors. There should be hardly any university in the world without power electronics in its electrical engineering curriculum.
